newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian call money ends higher, gilt prices fall.
newsitem.headline: Indian call money ends higher, gilt prices fall.

text.p: Indian call money ended Wednesday sharply higher at 10.50 percent against the day's opening levels of around 7.50 percent, dealers said.
Most of the day's deals were done between 10.25 percent and 10.85 percent, with a stray deal at 11 percent, they said.
Prices of government securities crashed in thin trade in the secondary market as some banks offloaded securities to raise cash, dealers said.
"As call money hardened, some banks chose to sell securities even at lower prices to meet their cash requirements," said a dealer at a foreign bank.

The 13.50 percent 1997 government of India stock was traded on Wednesday at 102.7 rupees against its last traded price of 103.25 rupees. The 13.62 percent 1998 stock shed 0.6 rupees to 103.8 while the 11.64 percent 2000 lost 0.95 rupees to 95.0.
Dealers were at a loss why the call rates hardened.

A half percentage point cut in banks' cash reserve requirements on Saturday injected around 21 billion rupees into the banking system while the reversal of a four-day repos held earlier in the week released a further 9.3 billions.
Dealers said call money rates should have come down in these circumstances.

One dealer said withdrawals from banks for cash expenditure during the festival season could have accounted for the shortage of funds. The Hindu new year was celebrated in different parts of the country between Sunday and Tuesday.
Other dealers said investments in treasury bills on tap with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) could have resulted in a diversion of funds from the call money market.
"Lenders seem to have invested surpluses in on-tap treasury bills," a dealer said. "This has resulted in a shortage of funds for lending in the call money market."

Aashish Pitale, manager debt research at ICICI Securities and Finance Company said a combination of open market operations by the RBI, pick up in bank credit disbursals and slowdown in deposits had caused the current hardening of rates.
Pitale said call rates should ease towards the end of the week when the on-tap treasury bills could be rediscounted with the RBI.
